title: Studio work, local big bands and free lessons
summary: Royal's present work in studios and Los Angeles big bands such as the Bossmen, and why he gives help but not paid lessons.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Well, do you do studio work (inaudible)?
Yes, I do studio work, uh-huh.
And you play with several bands around
town. You play with (inaudible) Bill Berry and you played with (inaudible) Nat Pierce and Frankie Capp
I play with three of the local bands here, the local big bands.
The new one that Frank de la Rosa and Harold Jones have.
And the new one, yeah, Right. They call themselves the Bossmen. They're --
Are you one of the leaders of that?
Sort of a cooperative or what? (inaudible)?

I end up somehow or other, I don't know how it happens, but it seems as though I end up sort of being the one that shows them how to do it with whatever damn band I get in, you know, so it's sort of that way. They ask me how this should be played and I end up giving them the tempos and the things. But I'm not the leader of it. I don't want to be the leader of anything.
It could be a headache, I know that.

I don't want to be. But I'll help them. If they need help, I'll give it. I give -- I don't have students because for me to teach what I know is, I really think, honestly, is so valuable that there's no way for me to put a monetary value on it. So, rather than have pupils, certain people, I give them free lessons and just show them, if they get hung up on something and don't know how to do it and they're all mixed up and trying to get themselves straight, I just tell them

to come to me and give me a list of what's wrong if they don't know what's happening and I usually give it to them for free. I don't teach or have any line of pupils or anything. I just give it out and try to help them out.
Marvelous opportunity, too, people who learn from you.

Yeah, but if I don't find a person that actually is sincere, and actually wants to do it, I won't bother with them at all. But by the same token, you find that sometimes a person has to pay for what they do before they will appreciate it, because a lot of times you give things for free and it's not appreciated. If you put a monetary value on it, then they will feel as though they've got to learn it, because they're paying for it, which is strictly a bad turnaround.
